title: Weekly paclitaxel + trastuzumab → trastuzumab continuation

agents.name: Paclitaxel
agents.explanation: Cells use tiny structures called microtubules to separate their chromosomes when dividing. Paclitaxel stabilises these structures so they cannot rearrange normally, interrupting cell division. It can also affect nerves and other healthy tissues.
agents.watch: Report tingling or numbness before the next weekly dose, especially if it affects walking or hand use. Tell the nurse immediately about flushing, chest or throat tightness, itching, dizziness or breathing changes during infusion.
risks: Hair loss, muscle or joint pain
Mouth, bowel, skin and nail effects

agents.name: Trastuzumab
agents.alias: IV infusion or locally approved subcutaneous injection every 3 weeks
agents.explanation: Trastuzumab binds to the HER2 protein on cells and helps reduce HER2-driven growth and recruit immune activity. HER2 testing identifies the cancers for which this approach is used.
agents.watch: Keep echo appointments throughout HER2 treatment. Report breathlessness, swelling, palpitations or a reaction; chemotherapy side effects are tracked separately.

context_label: Adjuvant HER2-positive, node-negative breast cancer; tumour ≤3 cm
purpose: Adjuvant treatment aims to reduce recurrence; confirm the exact treatment setting and sequence with your team.
schedule_summary: Paclitaxel weekly for 12 doses with trastuzumab every 3 weeks; continue trastuzumab to complete one year of HER2 treatment when appropriate. The team selects IV trastuzumab or locally approved subcutaneous trastuzumab; these are alternative formulations, not additional medicines.

phases_title: Each phase in your treatment plan
phases_note: The active phase determines the medicines and support prescription. Heart monitoring continues through the change to trastuzumab alone.
medicines_title: Your medicines and their different roles
timeline_note: Planned treatment days are distinct from broad possible symptom patterns. Symptoms can occur outside these bands.
safety_note: There are no guaranteed safe days. Fever, shivers, sudden illness, new breathing problems or severe symptoms need prompt advice on any day, including a treatment break.
teachback: Which medicines are due on which days? What symptoms mean you should call today? Which tests come next and who arranges them?
consent_support: Discuss the treatment setting, alternatives, exact schedule, common and serious drug-specific risks, fertility and pregnancy precautions, and the monitoring and urgent-contact plan.
urgent_extra: Contact oncology promptly for fever, shivering, unusual bleeding, severe mouth or bowel symptoms, inability to drink, reduced urine, new breathlessness or a painful/leaking line. Severe chest pain, collapse or severe breathing difficulty needs emergency help.

support.title: Anti-sickness plan
support.text: Follow the prevention and rescue instructions prescribed for this schedule. Call if vomiting prevents drinking.

support.title: Infection and bleeding
support.text: Know the local urgent-contact number. Fever, shivering, sudden illness or unusual bleeding needs prompt advice even between visits.

support.title: Medicine review
support.text: Show the oncology pharmacist all prescribed, over-the-counter and herbal medicines. Ask before starting anything new.

support.title: Premedicines belong to the active phase
support.text: Paclitaxel reaction medicines and AC anti-sickness medicines have different purposes. They are not automatically continued during trastuzumab-only treatment.

questions.q: Why is this schedule being recommended?
questions.a: This adjuvant option uses weekly paclitaxel with three-weekly trastuzumab for selected HER2-positive, node-negative cancers no larger than 3 cm. It avoids an anthracycline, but still requires heart monitoring and review for chemotherapy effects.

questions.q: What if a dose is missed or I feel unwell?
questions.a: Contact the unit for a revised plan. Do not double tablets, shift treatment dates or assume that an omitted dose should be made up.

items.title: Treatment setting
items.text: Adjuvant HER2-positive, node-negative breast cancer; tumour ≤3 cm

items.title: Your exact schedule
items.text: Paclitaxel weekly for 12 doses with trastuzumab every 3 weeks; continue trastuzumab to complete one year of HER2 treatment when appropriate. The team selects IV trastuzumab or locally approved subcutaneous trastuzumab; these are alternative formulations, not additional medicines.

items.title: Alternatives
items.text: Discuss suitable endocrine, targeted or chemotherapy options, expected benefit, practical demands and the option of supportive care according to your setting.

chapters.title: Checks across treatment
chapters.intro: Your clinical team books tests, reviews results and explains any change. Contact them if an expected test or instruction is missing.

items.title: Blood and kidney tests
items.text: Baseline blood tests and review before each chemotherapy administration according to the source and local plan. Once chemotherapy ends, testing follows trastuzumab and individual clinical needs.

items.title: Heart and breathing
items.text: Assess cardiac function before trastuzumab and every 12 weeks during treatment. Keep the same monitoring clock when paclitaxel ends or trastuzumab changes schedule; arrange earlier review for symptoms or falling function. EMA product information recommends cardiac checks every 6 months after treatment until 24 months; following anthracyclines in early disease, yearly up to 5 years from the last trastuzumab dose or longer if function falls. Your team individualises this plan.

items.title: Cancer imaging
items.text: After early-breast treatment, breast imaging and clinical review follow the agreed plan. Routine CT/PET scans or blood tumour markers are not used to look for distant recurrence in a person without symptoms or clinical concerns.

items.title: Bone health
items.text: Bone-density testing follows endocrine treatment, ovarian suppression, menopause and other bone-risk factors. DEXA is not automatically required before every chemotherapy course.

chapters.title: The wider treatment plan
chapters.intro: Follow the agreed early-breast pathway. Trastuzumab may continue after chemotherapy and can overlap radiotherapy when approved by the treating team. Endocrine therapy depends on hormone receptors.

items.title: When treatment changes
items.text: Reconcile active cancer medicines, supportive medicines and remaining symptoms before every transition.

items.title: Follow-up
items.text: Keep the agreed review appointments and report new symptoms between visits; this map does not detect missed tests.

items.title: Hormone treatment and bone care
items.text: Hormone-receptor results and your treatment setting determine whether endocrine therapy is appropriate. It has its own monitoring plan.

phases.label: Paclitaxel + trastuzumab
phases.detail: Weekly chemotherapy visits and three-weekly antibody visits overlap. Premedicines are linked to the paclitaxel dose.

phases.label: Trastuzumab alone
phases.detail: The chemotherapy stops. Heart monitoring continues on the existing schedule. This is adjuvant continuation, not metastatic maintenance.

steps.title: Before the first visit
steps.text: Blood tests, medicines review and the consent discussion come first. Confirm baseline and planned ongoing cardiac assessment.

steps.title: Plan venous access
steps.text: A cannula, PICC or implanted port may be used. If a port is chosen, a trained team inserts it in a separate procedure with local anaesthetic and sometimes sedation; the team explains fasting, blood-thinner and wound instructions.

steps.title: Infusion day
steps.text: Paclitaxel is an IV infusion. Trastuzumab may be IV or, if locally approved and prescribed, a subcutaneous injection. Staff confirm formulation, observation and access needs at every phase change.

steps.title: Home and next review
steps.text: This regimen does not routinely need a take-home infusion pump. Staff disconnect the infusion; a port is de-accessed when appropriate. Keep line-care and next-visit instructions.

details.title: Port insertion and removal
details.text: The line team explains placement, dressing care and when normal activities can resume. A port is accessed with a special needle during treatment. Removal of the implanted device is a separate planned procedure when no longer needed; do not remove or adjust it yourself.

details.title: PICC care and urgent line symptoms
details.text: A PICC usually needs regular dressing and flushing appointments even between treatments. Fever, redness, swelling, pain, leakage or damage requires prompt advice. Your hospital supplies the exact care instructions.

details.title: Visit time and transport
details.text: First visits can take longer because of loading doses, premedicines and observation. Ask the unit about expected time, transport and any escort needed after sedation or line insertion.

details.title: Phase-specific visit pattern
details.text: Paclitaxel weekly for 12 doses with trastuzumab every 3 weeks; continue trastuzumab to complete one year of HER2 treatment when appropriate. The team selects IV trastuzumab or locally approved subcutaneous trastuzumab; these are alternative formulations, not additional medicines. No take-home infusion pump is part of this schedule. Port de-accessing after a visit is different from removal of the implanted port.

anatomy: Hair loss or thinning varies; ask about support.
Painful ulcers or difficulty drinking need advice.
New cough or breathlessness needs prompt assessment.
New chest pain, fainting or severe breathlessness needs urgent assessment.
Report diarrhoea early, especially with poor intake or dizziness.
Report numbness, tingling or pain affecting daily activity.
Fever, shivers, unusual bleeding or sudden illness: call promptly.
Report severe rash, blistering or yellow skin / eyes promptly.
